## Key points about the Unix Shell I

::: {.incremental}

- **What is Unix?**  
  Unix is a family of operating systems that started at Bell Labs in 1969 and still shapes most of today's computing. Linux and macOS are its descendants or close relatives. Its design philosophy: build small programs that each do one thing well, treat almost everything as a file, and use plain text as the common language between programs.

- **What is the Unix shell?**  
  The shell is a program that reads the commands you type and asks the operating system to run other programs for you. It is both an interactive interface (you type, it answers) and a scripting language (you save the same commands in a file to repeat them). Common shells are `bash` and `zsh`, and `zsh` is the default on modern macOS.

:::

## Key points about the Unix Shell II

::: {.incremental}

- **How is the shell different from Python or R?**  
  Python and R are built to *compute*; the shell is built to *connect* existing programs. A few things set it apart:
  - The commands you type interactively are the same ones you put in a script, so there is no switch between "exploring" and "automating".
  - Wildcards let one line act on thousands of files: `wc -l *.csv` counts the lines in every CSV file in the folder.
  - Any program, in any language, can be a building block.

- **One tiny symbol made Unix incredibly powerful: `|`**  
  The pipe sends the output of one command to the input of the next, like an assembly line for data. 

:::

## Key points about the Unix Shell III

::: {.incremental}

- **Why it matters for researchers today**  
  - **Remote machines:** university clusters and supercomputers (all of the world's top 500 run Linux) are usually reached *only* through a shell.
  - **Scale:** you can inspect a 50 GB file with `head`, `wc`, or `grep` without opening it, and run the same analysis over hundreds of samples with a loop.
  - **Reproducibility:** a shell script is a precise, re-runnable record of what you did to your data.
  - **Longevity:** commands from the 1970s still work today, so the skills you learn won't expire.

:::

## Unix, Shell, Terminal, Bash : What’s the Difference?

<!-- Source slide 5 -->

These terms are often used interchangeably, but they refer to distinct layers of the system.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="51%"}
![Stack diagram showing Unix, shell, terminal, Bash](images/unix-shell-introduction/slide-05-01-012397bbd5.png){width="96%"}
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
**Breaking it down**

**Unix** — The operating system itself: the foundation everything runs on.

**Shell** — The “language” used to send commands to the OS.

**Terminal** — The application window where you interact with the shell.

**Bash** — A specific, widely used implementation of a Unix shell.
:::
:::


## What you’ll use today {.spacious-slide}



::: {.fragment}

- **Git Bash (for windows users)** 🪟 

A lightweight Bash emulation that comes bundled with Git for Windows. It gives you a Unix-like environment on a Windows machine.

:::


::: {.fragment}

- **Unix shell (for the rest)** 🍎 /🐧 

The classic, native command-line environment. macOS and Linux ship with Bash (or Zsh) built right in. No extra installation needed.

:::

## Meet Nelle Nemo, Our case study

<!-- Source slide 10 -->

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
![Marine biologist at work](images/unix-shell-introduction/slide-10-01-64ed3dd2e1.png){width="77%"}
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
**Who is Nelle?**

Nelle Nemo is a marine biologist who has collected thousands of biological samples. She needs to process **1,520 files**, and doing it by hand would take weeks.

**By the end of this lesson, you'll have the skills to help her:**

- Navigate directories and files
- Create and organize data
- Chain commands together
- Automate tasks with loops and scripts
- Search efficiently through files
:::
:::
